}\n    .cols { display: block; }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n\n<a class=\"skip\" href=\"#main\">Skip to main content</a>\n\n<div class=\"shell\">\n  <header class=\"hero\">\n    <p class=\"eyebrow\">Research paper</p>\n    <h1>Pre-Registered Screening of Internal Safety Metrics for Language Model Checkpoints</h1>\n    <p class=\"byline\">Anonymous</p>\n    <p class=\"tldr\">\n      Open-weight language models proliferate faster than anyone can evaluate them for safety. We asked whether a metric computable from a single checkpoint, using at most 16 prompts and no text generation, could rank models by safety without running a full benchmark. We screened 14 candidate internal metrics on 23 chat models from 8 architecture families against a two-sided safety score that penalises both harmful compliance and over-refusal. Under six selection rules frozen before scoring, one candidate passed: <strong>twin d-prime (C12)</strong>, which measures how well a model's mid-layer activations separate harmful from safe prompts, with Spearman rho = 0.61 against balanced safety. The strongest raw correlation belonged to self-ablation sensitivity (C2, rho = 0.90), but no internal metric added significant information beyond generating and judging just 16 completions.\n    </p>\n    <div class=\"actions\">\n      <a class=\"btn btn-primary\" href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-87348a-cheap-safety-metrics-you-could-still@main/paper.pdf\">Read the Paper (PDF)</a>\n      <a class=\"btn btn-ghost\" href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-87348a-cheap-safety-metrics-you-could-still\">Code Repository</a>\n    </div>\n  </header>\n\n  <div class=\"cols\">\n    <nav class=\"sidenav\" aria-label=\"Section navigation\">\n      <h2>Contents</h2>\n      <ol>\n        <li><a href=\"#contributions\">Contributions</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#method\">Method</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#results\">Results</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#figures\">Figures</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#limitations\">Limitations</a></li>\n      </ol>\n    </nav>\n\n    <main id=\"main\">\n\n      <!-- ============ CONTRIBUTIONS ============ -->\n      <section id=\"contributions\" aria-labelledby=\"h-contributions\">\n        <span class=\"sec-mark\">01</span>\n        <h2 id=\"h-contributions\">Contributions</h2>\n        <p class=\"sec-lede\">Five results, stated as the evidence supports them.</p>\n\n        <div class=\"cards\">\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">01</span>\n            <h3>The Screen</h3>\n            <p>14 of 16 registered candidate metrics executed on 23 graded checkpoints from 8 architecture families. Under six selection rules, one candidate passes all six: twin d-prime (C12, rho = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]). Self-ablation sensitivity (C2, rho = 0.90) clears amended rules, but its three surviving variants (C2, C2n, C17) are monotone transforms of one measurement.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">02</span>\n            <h3>Two-Sided Ground Truth</h3>\n            <p>23 checkpoints scored on the 94-item CORE-94 set (66 harmful, 28 XSTest-safe) with 64-token greedy decoding and a Gemini-2.5-Flash stance judge. A secondary judge (GPT-5-mini) agrees at kappa = 0.72. A blanket refuser scores S<sub>2</sub> = 0.5, not 1.0.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">03</span>\n            <h3>AMS Incumbent Comparison</h3>\n            <p>Every variant of the published AMS metric correlates worse than C2 with two-sided safety, with paired confidence intervals excluding zero. The reference implementation (ams-scanner 0.1.3) contains a right-padding bug that reads PAD-token activations.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">04</span>\n            <h3>Content-Free Pull Control</h3>\n            <p>After subtracting a norm-matched random steer from C1, the corrected metric (C1n) correlates at rho = 0.76, essentially unchanged (rho(C1, C1n) = 0.995), refuting the hypothesis that C1's signal is a content-free pull toward refusal.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">05</span>\n            <h3>Grader-Side Refusal</h3>\n            <p>LLM judges under the StrongREJECT rubric assign the degenerate score tuple (1,1,1) to 65.9% of harmful items, with 328 vs. 67 discordant items against a stance-based framing (McNemar p &lt; 10<sup>-42</sup>).</p>\n          </article>\n        </div>\n      </section>\n\n      <!-- ============ METHOD ============ -->\n      <section id=\"method\" aria-labelledby=\"h-method\">\n        <span class=\"sec-mark\">02</span>\n        <h2 id=\"h-method\">Method</h2>\n        <p class=\"sec-lede\">One checkpoint in, one number out, with the ground truth and the rules fixed before any candidate was scored.</p>\n\n        <figure>\n          <button type=\"button\" class=\"figframe\" data-fig=\"0\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: pipeline overview\">\n            <img src=\"figures/fig_overview_v0.jpg\" alt=\"Pipeline diagram: 16 pre-registered candidate metrics, 14 of them executed, read weights or activations from each of 23 graded checkpoints on the 16-prompt SCREEN16 set; in parallel the CORE-94 set of 94 prompts is generated at 64 tokens and scored by a stance judge into the balanced safety target; six selection rules then filter the candidates down to one survivor, C12.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n          </button>\n          <figcaption><b>Pipeline overview.</b> Candidates read a single checkpoint on at most 16 prompts; the target is scored separately by generation and judging; six frozen rules decide what survives.</figcaption>\n        </figure>\n\n        <h3>Two-sided ground truth</h3>\n        <p>The target is balanced safety: S<sub>2</sub> = 0.5 &times; (harm-refusal rate) + 0.5 &times; (benign-compliance rate), computed on CORE-94, a set of 66 harmful items and 28 XSTest-safe items. Both failure modes cost the same. A model that refuses everything scores 0.5, and so does a model that complies with everything. That is the point of the two-sidedness: a one-sided refusal rate would reward a blanket refuser with a perfect score.</p>\n\n        <h3>Panel</h3>\n        <p>36 checkpoints from 8 architecture families (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, TinyLlama, Llama-3.2, OLMo-2, SmolLM2, Falcon3, Danube3), of which 23 are graded. All are at most 4B parameters and run in bf16, which is what makes a panel of this width affordable at all.</p>\n\n        <h3>Candidates</h3>\n        <p>16 candidate metrics in 7 families. Each one reads hidden states or weights on at most 16 prompts, the SCREEN16 set, and none of them generates text. Two behavioural quantities enter as bars rather than as candidates: the logit gap and refusal mass. A candidate has to beat them, not merely correlate.</p>\n\n        <h3>Six selection rules</h3>\n        <ol class=\"plain\">\n          <li><b>S1, incremental signal.</b> The candidate adds information beyond the cheap behavioural bars.</li>\n          <li><b>S2, direction specificity.</b> The signal is tied to the harm direction, not to any direction.</li>\n          <li><b>S3, pole control.</b> The metric responds to the safety pole rather than to generic prompt structure.</li>\n          <li><b>S4, sign agreement.</b> The correlation points the same way across subsets.</li>\n          <li><b>S5, efficiency.</b> The read is cheap enough to be worth doing.</li>\n          <li><b>S6, beyond confounds.</b> The relation survives known nuisance variables.</li>\n        </ol>\n        <p>The rules were frozen before scoring. That is what lets a single survivor mean something: C12 was not chosen after looking at which candidate won.</p>\n      </section>\n\n      <!-- ============ RESULTS ============ -->\n      <section id=\"results\" aria-labelledby=\"h-results\">\n        <span class=\"sec-mark\">03</span>\n        <h2 id=\"h-results\">Results</h2>\n        <p class=\"sec-lede\">One metric passes every rule. A different metric correlates far better and fails on specificity. Neither beats the behavioural ceiling.</p>\n\n        <div class=\"statgrid\">\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">0.61</span><span class=\"lbl\">C12 rho against balanced safety [0.36, 0.87]</span></div>\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">0.90</span><span class=\"lbl\">C2 rho, strongest raw correlation [0.79, 0.97]</span></div>\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">0.93</span><span class=\"lbl\">rho of 16 judged completions with full CORE-94</span></div>\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">1 of 14</span><span class=\"lbl\">executed candidates passing all six rules</span></div>\n        </div>\n\n        <h3>The sole survivor</h3>\n        <p>C12, twin d-prime, reaches rho = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87] against balanced safety, with partial rho = 0.43 and a one-sided bound of 0.006. It is the only candidate to clear all six pre-registered rules.</p>\n        <p>The within-family picture is mixed in a way worth stating plainly. C12 is significant within Qwen3 (rho = 0.67, n = 8) and within Qwen2.5 (rho = 0.70, n = 5). It is not within TinyLlama (rho = -0.10, n = 5). A metric that works inside two families and reverses sign inside a third is not yet a general instrument.</p>\n\n        <figure>\n          <button type=\"button\" class=\"figframe\" data-fig=\"1\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: C12 twin d-prime versus balanced safety\">\n            <img src=\"figures/fig_c12_scatter_v0.png\" alt=\"Scatter plot of C12 twin d-prime on the horizontal axis against balanced safety S2 on the vertical axis for 23 graded checkpoints, with points coloured by architecture family; the cloud rises to the right with substantial spread, and values are spread across the range rather than clustered at zero.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n          </button>\n          <figcaption><b>C12 twin d-prime vs balanced safety.</b> Scatter plot of C12 (twin d-prime) versus balanced safety (S<sub>2</sub>) for the 23 graded checkpoints, coloured by architecture family. C12 is the sole candidate to pass all six selection rules, with Spearman rho = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]. Unlike C2, C12's values are more evenly distributed: 12 of 23 models exceed the random-direction null.</figcaption>\n        </figure>\n\n        <h3>The strongest correlation</h3>\n        <p>C2, self-ablation sensitivity, reaches rho = 0.90 [0.79, 0.97], and exceeds the logit gap by 0.128 [0.012, 0.410]. As a detector of models with an ablatable harm direction it reaches AUROC = 0.96. But its distribution is close to binary, and within the 10 models that exceed the null the restricted correlation falls to rho = 0.64. C2 is largely telling you whether a harm direction exists to ablate, and only secondarily how safe the model is.</p>\n\n        <figure>\n          <button type=\"button\" class=\"figframe\" data-fig=\"2\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: C2 self-ablation versus balanced safety\">\n            <img src=\"figures/fig_screen_scatter_v0.png\" alt=\"Scatter plot of C2 self-ablation sensitivity on the horizontal axis against balanced safety S2 on the vertical axis for 23 graded checkpoints, coloured by architecture family; a dense cluster of points sits near zero on the left and a separate group lies to the right of a dashed vertical line marking absolute C2 equal to 0.1.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n          </button>\n          <figcaption><b>C2 self-ablation vs balanced safety.</b> Scatter plot of C2 (self-ablation sensitivity) versus balanced safety (S<sub>2</sub>) for the 23 graded checkpoints. Points are coloured by architecture family. C2 achieves Spearman rho = 0.90 [0.79, 0.97]. The plot reveals a near-binary split: 10 of 23 models have |C2| &gt; 0.1 (right cluster), while 13 cluster near zero. <main id="main">

<!-- HERO -->
<section id="hero" class="hero">
  <div class="container">
    <h1>One Candidate Survives: A Pre-Registered Screen of Internal Safety Metrics for Language Model Checkpoints</h1>
    <p class="author">Anonymous</p>
    <p class="tldr">
      Open-weight language models proliferate faster than anyone can evaluate them for safety.
      We asked whether a metric computable from a single checkpoint, using at most 16 prompts and
      no text generation, could rank models by safety without running a full benchmark. We screened
      14 candidate internal metrics on 23 chat models from 8 architecture families against a two-sided
      safety score that penalises both harmful compliance and over-refusal. Under six selection rules
      frozen before scoring, one candidate passed: twin d-prime (C12), which measures how well a
      model's mid-layer activations separate harmful from safe prompts, with Spearman &#961; = 0.61
      against balanced safety. The strongest raw correlation belonged to self-ablation sensitivity
      (C2, &#961; = 0.90), but no internal metric added significant information beyond generating
      and judging just 16 completions.
    </p>
    <div class="hero-links">
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-87348a-cheap-safety-metrics-you-could-still@main/paper.pdf" class="hero-link hero-link--primary">Read the Paper (PDF)</a>
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-87348a-cheap-safety-metrics-you-could-still" class="hero-link hero-link--secondary">Code Repository</a>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->
<section id="contributions">
  <div class="container">
    <h2>Contributions</h2>
    <div class="card-grid">
      <div class="card">
        <h3>The Screen</h3>
        <p>14 of 16 registered candidate metrics executed on 23 graded checkpoints from 8 architecture families. Under six selection rules, one candidate passes all six: twin d-prime (C12, &#961; = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]). Self-ablation sensitivity (C2, &#961; = 0.90) clears amended rules, but its three surviving variants (C2, C2n, C17) are monotone transforms of one measurement.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Two-Sided Ground Truth</h3>
        <p>23 checkpoints scored on the 94-item CORE-94 set (66 harmful, 28 XSTest-safe) with 64-token greedy decoding and a Gemini-2.5-Flash stance judge. A secondary judge (GPT-5-mini) agrees at &#954; = 0.72. Under S&#8322;, a blanket refuser scores 0.5, not 1.0.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>AMS Incumbent Comparison</h3>
        <p>Every variant of the published AMS metric correlates worse than C2 with two-sided safety, with paired confidence intervals excluding zero. The reference implementation (ams-scanner 0.1.3) contains a right-padding bug that reads PAD-token activations.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Content-Free Pull Control</h3>
        <p>After subtracting a norm-matched random steer from C1, the corrected metric (C1n) correlates at &#961; = 0.76, essentially unchanged (&#961;(C1, C1n) = 0.995), refuting the hypothesis that C1's signal is a content-free pull toward refusal.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Grader-Side Refusal</h3>
        <p>LLM judges under the StrongREJECT rubric assign the degenerate score tuple (1, 1, 1) to 65.9% of harmful items, with 328 vs. 67 discordant items against a stance-based framing (McNemar p &lt; 10<sup>-42</sup>).</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- METHOD -->
<section id="method">
  <div class="container">
    <h2>Method</h2>

    <figure class="method-figure">
      <img src="figures/fig_overview_v0.jpg" alt="Pipeline overview diagram showing three stages: a checkpoint panel of 36 models from 8 families feeds into ground-truth scoring on CORE-94 with a stance judge, and 16 candidate metrics feed into a pre-registered screen with 6 selection rules, producing one survivor C12 with rho 0.61.">
      <figcaption>Overview of the cheap safety metric screening pipeline. Sixteen candidate metrics are pre-registered and fourteen are executed on 23 graded checkpoints from 8 architecture families. Each metric reads a single checkpoint's weights or activations on at most 16 prompts (the SCREEN16 set). Ground truth is two-sided balanced safety (S&#8322;), scored on the 94-item CORE-94 set with 64-token greedy decoding and a Gemini-2.5-Flash stance judge. Six selection rules filter candidates; one candidate (C12, twin d-prime) passes all six.</figcaption>
    </figure>

    <h3>Two-sided ground truth</h3>
    <p>
      Existing safety metrics evaluate on one-sided ground truth: they measure whether a model refuses harmful prompts but ignore whether it complies with benign ones. A blanket refuser scores perfectly on harm-refusal rate but is useless. The balanced safety score corrects this:
    </p>
    <div class="formula">
      S&#8322; = 0.5 &times; (harm-refusal rate on 66 harmful items) + 0.5 &times; (1 &minus; false-refusal rate on 28 XSTest-safe items)
    </div>
    <p>
      Under S&#8322;, a blanket refuser scores 0.5, not 1.0. The item set is CORE-94: 66 harmful-side items (from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and XSTest contrast items) and 28 XSTest-safe items (benign prompts phrased to resemble harmful ones). Completions are generated with greedy decoding at 64 new tokens and judged by Gemini-2.5-Flash using a stance-based framing. A secondary judge (GPT-5-mini) agrees at &#954; = 0.72 (agreement 86.3%, n = 525 items).
    </p>

    <h3>Panel</h3>
    <p>
      36 checkpoints from 8 architecture families (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, TinyLlama, Llama-3.2, OLMo-2, SmolLM2, Falcon3, Danube3) spanning 11 lineages. All are at most 4B parameters and load in bf16. Of these, 23 are graded with two-sided labels, 12 are ungraded, and 1 is a base model. At the panel's realised size (n = 23, ICC = 0.103), the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is |&#961;| = 0.53.
    </p>

    <h3>Candidate metrics</h3>
    <p>
      16 candidates grouped into seven conceptual families, each reading hidden states or weights of a single model on at most 16 prompts (the frozen SCREEN16 set of 8 harmful/benign-twin pairs). Candidates range from causal gain measures (C1-C3) and component routing (C6-C9) to two-sided geometry (C12-C13) and a learned ridge metamodel (C14). The first-token logit gap and refusal-token mass enter as baselines, never as eligible survivors.
    </p>

    <h3>Selection rules</h3>
    <p>A candidate passes the screen if it satisfies all six rules, hashed before scoring:</p>
    <ul class="rules-list">
      <li data-rule="S1">Incremental signal: partial &#961; with S&#8322; (removing logit gap and model size) excludes zero.</li>
      <li data-rule="S2">Direction specificity: within-lineage permutation p &lt; 0.05 and metric exceeds its random-direction null on a majority of the panel.</li>
      <li data-rule="S3">Pole control: both always-refuse and never-refuse wrappers score worse than the honest instruct checkpoint from the same family.</li>
      <li data-rule="S4">Sign agreement: same sign at checkpoint and family aggregation.</li>
      <li data-rule="S5">Efficiency: at most 16 prompts and under 2 minutes per ~4B model.</li>
      <li data-rule="S6">Beyond confounds: beats family-only and size-only out-of-fold predictors.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- RESULTS -->
<section id="results">
  <div class="container">
    <h2>Results</h2>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>The sole survivor: C12 (twin d-prime)</h3>
      <div class="stat-row">
        <div class="stat">
          <div class="stat-value">&#961; = 0.61</div>
          <div class="stat-label">Spearman with S&#8322; [0.36, 0.87]</div>
        </div>
        <div class="stat">
          <div class="stat-value">0.43</div>
          <div class="stat-label">Partial &#961; (bound 0.006)</div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <p>
        C12 is the sole candidate to pass all six selection rules. It measures how well a model's mid-layer activations separate harmful from safe prompts via a cross-fitted harm axis. C12 is significant within Qwen3 (&#961; = 0.67, n = 8) and Qwen2.5 (&#961; = 0.70, n = 5) but not TinyLlama (&#961; = -0.10, n = 5). Of 23 models, 12 exceed the random-direction null, more evenly distributed across the safety range than C2's pattern.
      </p>
      <figure class="result-figure">
        <img src="figures/fig_c12_scatter_v0.png"
             alt="Scatter plot of C12 twin d-prime versus balanced safety S2 for 23 checkpoints coloured by architecture family, showing a positive correlation of rho 0.61 with points spread across the range."
             tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge C12 scatter plot"
             data-full="figures/fig_c12_scatter_v0.png"
             data-caption="Scatter plot of C12 (twin d-prime) versus balanced safety (S&#8322;) for the 23 graded checkpoints, coloured by architecture family. C12 is the sole candidate to pass all six selection rules, with Spearman &#961; = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]. Unlike C2, C12's values are more evenly distributed: 12 of 23 models exceed the random-direction null.">
        <figcaption>C12 (twin d-prime) versus balanced safety. Spearman &#961; = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]. Points coloured by architecture family; 12 of 23 models exceed the random-direction null.</figcaption>
      </figure>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>The strongest correlation: C2 (self-ablation sensitivity)</h3>
      <div class="stat-row">
        <div class="stat">
          <div class="stat-value">&#961; = 0.90</div>
          <div class="stat-label">Spearman with S&#8322; [0.79, 0.97]</div>
        </div>
        <div class="stat">
          <div class="stat-value">AUROC 0.96</div>
          <div class="stat-label">Detection of ablatable harm direction</div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <p>
        C2 exceeds the logit gap (&#961; = 0.77) by a paired difference of 0.128 [0.012, 0.410], which excludes zero. C2 is significant within all three large families (Qwen3: &#961; = 0.95; Qwen2.5: &#961; = 1.00; TinyLlama: &#961; = 1.00), while the logit gap reaches significance in only two. However, the correlation partly reflects a near-binary split: only 10 of 23 models have |C2| > 0.1, and models exceeding their random-direction null cluster in the safer half of the panel. Within the 10 models exceeding the null, restricted &#961; = 0.64.
      </p>
      <p>
        C2, C2n, and C17 are monotone functions of the same self-ablation measurement. Shipping three survivors satisfies the letter of a "three independent metrics" requirement but not its spirit.
      </p>
      <figure class="result-figure">
        <img src="figures/fig_screen_scatter_v0.png"
             alt="Scatter plot of C2 self-ablation sensitivity versus balanced safety S2 for 23 checkpoints showing a strong positive correlation of rho 0.90 with a binary split at C2 equals 0.1."
             tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge C2 scatter plot"
             data-full="figures/fig_screen_scatter_v0.png"
             data-caption="Scatter plot of C2 (self-ablation sensitivity) versus balanced safety (S&#8322;) for the 23 graded checkpoints. Points are coloured by architecture family. C2 achieves Spearman &#961; = 0.90 [0.79, 0.97]. The plot reveals a near-binary split: 10 of 23 models have |C2| > 0.1 (right cluster), while 13 cluster near zero. The dashed vertical line marks |C2| = 0.1.">
        <figcaption>C2 (self-ablation sensitivity) versus balanced safety. Spearman &#961; = 0.90 [0.79, 0.97]. Dashed lines mark |C2| = 0.1; 10 of 23 models fall outside that band.</figcaption>
      </figure>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>AMS incumbent comparison</h3>
      <p>
        Every variant of the published AMS metric correlates worse than C2, with confidence intervals excluding zero. Four of five variants also lose to the first-token logit gap.
      </p>
      <div class="table-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead>
            <tr>
              <th>AMS Variant</th>
              <th>&#961;</th>
              <th>vs. C2 [CI]</th>
              <th>vs. Logit Gap [CI]</th>
            </tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>AMS_published</td><td class="num">0.28</td><td class="num">-0.62 [-1.01, -0.25]</td><td class="num">-0.49 [-0.92, -0.08]</td></tr>
            <tr><td>AMS_mean3</td><td class="num">0.50</td><td class="num">-0.40 [-0.68, -0.07]</td><td class="num">-0.28 [-0.54, +0.01]</td></tr>
            <tr><td>AMS_cf_layer</td><td class="num">0.33</td><td class="num">-0.57 [-0.83, -0.17]</td><td class="num">-0.44 [-0.69, -0.08]</td></tr>
            <tr><td>AMS_cf_sweep</td><td class="num">0.21</td><td class="num">-0.69 [-1.05, -0.33]</td><td class="num">-0.56 [-0.93, -0.16]</td></tr>
            <tr><td>AMS_screen16</td><td class="num">0.48</td><td class="num">-0.42 [-0.66, -0.14]</td><td class="num">-0.29 [-0.50, -0.01]</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p style="font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin-top: 0.5rem;">
        Paired lineage-bootstrap &#961;-differences on the balanced target (n = 23). Negative = AMS variant is worse. All AMS variants fail S5 (96 prompts > 16 limit).
      </p>
      <p>
        The reference implementation ams-scanner 0.1.3 reads <code>hidden_states[:,-1,:]</code> on right-padded batches, extracting PAD-token activations rather than the last real token. On Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, this changes the AMS &#963; from 5.33 (correct) to 0.74 (the package default), flipping the verdict from PASS to CRITICAL.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>The ceiling: 16 judged completions</h3>
      <div class="stat-row">
        <div class="stat">
          <div class="stat-value">&#961; = 0.93</div>
          <div class="stat-label">16 judged completions vs. full CORE-94</div>
        </div>
        <div class="stat">
          <div class="stat-value">~16 s</div>
          <div class="stat-label">Internal read per 4B model</div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <p>
        The model's own judged behaviour on 16 SCREEN16 items achieves &#961; = 0.93 [0.75, 0.97] with the full CORE-94 target. Given this probe, no internal read adds significant information: C2 adds partial &#961; = 0.31 (bound -0.12); C12 adds -0.01 (bound -0.27). An internal metric roughly matches the information in 16 judged completions but has not been shown to exceed it. The practical advantage is cost: about 16 seconds per 4B model, no LLM judge needed.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>The logit gap as floor</h3>
      <p>
        The first-token logit gap (&#961; = 0.77) requires no internal access and costs one forward pass per prompt. It fails only S3 (pole control) among the rules it is eligible for. C2 significantly exceeds the logit gap (&#916;&#961; = 0.13 [0.01, 0.41]), but C12 does not (&#916;&#961; = -0.17 [-0.47, 0.19]). The logit gap is blind to TinyLlama (&#961; = 0.00), and C2's advantage there (&#961; = 1.00) is the strongest argument for internal reads.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- FIGURE GALLERY -->
<section id="figures">
  <div class="wide-container">
    <h2>Figures</h2>
    <div class="gallery-grid">

      <div class="gallery-item" tabindex="0" role="button"
           aria-label="Enlarge pipeline overview figure"
           data-full="figures/fig_overview_v0.jpg"
           data-caption="Overview of the cheap safety metric screening pipeline. Sixteen candidate metrics are pre-registered and fourteen are executed on 23 graded checkpoints from 8 architecture families. Each metric reads a single checkpoint's weights or activations on at most 16 prompts (the SCREEN16 set). Ground truth is two-sided balanced safety (S&#8322;), scored on the 94-item CORE-94 set with 64-token greedy decoding and a Gemini-2.5-Flash stance judge. Six selection rules filter candidates; one candidate (C12, twin d-prime) passes all six.">
        <img src="figures/fig_overview_v0.jpg" alt="Pipeline overview diagram showing three stages: checkpoint panel, ground-truth scoring on CORE-94, and a pre-registered screen with 6 selection rules producing one survivor C12.">

Unlike C2, C12's values are more evenly distributed: 12 of 23 models exceed the random-direction null.">
        <img src="figures/fig_c12_scatter_v0.png" alt="Scatter plot of C12 twin d-prime versus balanced safety for 23 checkpoints coloured by family, showing positive correlation rho 0.61 with points spread across the range.">

<!-- LIMITATIONS -->
<section id="limitations">
  <div class="container">
    <h2>Limitations</h2>
    <ul class="limitations-list">
      <li>The panel covers only models at or below 4B parameters with publicly available safetensors. Whether the results generalise to larger models or proprietary architectures is unknown.</li>
      <li>The prompt set is limited to English single-turn interactions; multi-turn and multilingual safety are not tested.</li>
      <li>C4 and C5 (direction-conditioned weight paths) were not executed.</li>
      <li>The ROSI reversal is tested on one checkpoint at 128 tokens and two checkpoints at 20 tokens.</li>
      <li>The confirmation test on blind Set A checkpoints has not been run: no safety labels exist for the frozen Set A models. Until confirmation, the screen remains exploratory.</li>
      <li>The 16-prompt judged behavioural probe (&#961; = 0.93) remains the ceiling. No internal metric adds significant predictive power beyond generating and judging 16 completions.</li>
      <li>Standard safety benchmarks (TrustLLM, AIR-Bench, HELM-Safety) have zero coverage on this panel. External validation is limited to harm-refusal rate (n = 23) and OLB2 (n = 8, descriptive).</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</section>

<script>
(function() {
  // -- Section navigation highlighting --
  var navLinks = document.querySelectorAll('.nav-link[data-section]');
  var sections = [];
  navLinks.forEach(function(link) {
    var sec = document.getElementById(link.dataset.section);
    if (sec) sections.push({ el: sec, link: link });
  });

  function updateNav() {
    var scrollY = window.scrollY + 80;
    var current = sections[0];
    for (var i = 0; i < sections.length; i++) {
      if (sections[i].el.offsetTop <= scrollY) current = sections[i];
    }
    navLinks.forEach(function(l) { l.classList.remove('active'); });
    if (current) current.link.classList.add('active');
  }

  var ticking = false;
  window.addEventListener('scroll', function() {
    if (!ticking) {
      requestAnimationFrame(function() { updateNav(); ticking = false; });
      ticking = true;
    }
  });
  updateNav();

  // -- Lightbox --
  var lightbox = document.getElementById('lightbox');
  var lbImg = document.getElementById('lightbox-img');
  var lbCaption = document.getElementById('lightbox-caption');
  var lbClose = lightbox.querySelector('.lightbox-close');
  var lastFocus = null;

  function openLightbox(src, alt, caption) {
    lastFocus = document.activeElement;
    lbImg.src = src;
    lbImg.alt = alt;
    lbCaption.innerHTML = caption || '';
    lightbox.classList.add('open');
    lbClose.focus();
    document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';
  }

  function closeLightbox() {
    lightbox.classList.remove('open');
    lbImg.src = '';
    document.body.style.overflow = '';
    if (lastFocus) lastFocus.focus();
  }

  lbClose.addEventListener('click', closeLightbox);
  lightbox.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
    if (e.target === lightbox) closeLightbox();
  });
  document.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
    if (e.key === 'Escape' && lightbox.classList.contains('open')) {
      closeLightbox();
    }
  });

  // Focus trap
  lightbox.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
    if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
    var focusable = lightbox.querySelectorAll('button, [tabindex="0"]');
    if (focusable.length === 0) return;
    var first = focusable[0];
    var last = focusable[focusable.length - 1];
    if (e.shiftKey) {
      if (document.activeElement === first) { e.preventDefault(); last.focus(); }
    } else {
      if (document.activeElement === last) { e.preventDefault(); first.focus(); }
    }
  });

  // Gallery items
  document.querySelectorAll('.gallery-item').forEach(function(item) {
    function activate() {
      var img = item.querySelector('img');
      openLightbox(item.dataset.full, img.alt, item.dataset.caption);
    }
    item.addEventListener('click', activate);
    item.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
      if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); activate(); }
    });
  });

  // Result figures
  document.querySelectorAll('.result-figure img[data-full]').forEach(function(img) {
    function activate() {
      openLightbox(img.dataset.full, img.alt, img.dataset.caption);
    }
    img.addEventListener('click', activate);
    img.addEventListener('keydown', function(e) {
      if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); activate(); }
    });
  });
})();
</script>

</body>

}\n    .cols { display: block; }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n\n<a class=\"skip\" href=\"#main\">Skip to main content</a>\n\n<div class=\"shell\">\n  <header class=\"hero\">\n    <p class=\"eyebrow\">Research paper</p>\n    <h1>Pre-Registered Screening of Internal Safety Metrics for Language Model Checkpoints</h1>\n    <p class=\"byline\">Anonymous</p>\n    <p class=\"tldr\">\n      Open-weight language models proliferate faster than anyone can evaluate them for safety. We asked whether a metric computable from a single checkpoint, using at most 16 prompts and no text generation, could rank models by safety without running a full benchmark. We screened 14 candidate internal metrics on 23 chat models from 8 architecture families against a two-sided safety score that penalises both harmful compliance and over-refusal. Under six selection rules frozen before scoring, one candidate passed: <strong>twin d-prime (C12)</strong>, which measures how well a model's mid-layer activations separate harmful from safe prompts, with Spearman rho = 0.61 against balanced safety. The strongest raw correlation belonged to self-ablation sensitivity (C2, rho = 0.90), but no internal metric added significant information beyond generating and judging just 16 completions.\n    </p>\n    <div class=\"actions\">\n      <a class=\"btn btn-primary\" href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-87348a-cheap-safety-metrics-you-could-still@main/paper.pdf\">Read the Paper (PDF)</a>\n      <a class=\"btn btn-ghost\" href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-87348a-cheap-safety-metrics-you-could-still\">Code Repository</a>\n    </div>\n  </header>\n\n  <div class=\"cols\">\n    <nav class=\"sidenav\" aria-label=\"Section navigation\">\n      <h2>Contents</h2>\n      <ol>\n        <li><a href=\"#contributions\">Contributions</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#method\">Method</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#results\">Results</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#figures\">Figures</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#limitations\">Limitations</a></li>\n      </ol>\n    </nav>\n\n    <main id=\"main\">\n\n      <!-- ============ CONTRIBUTIONS ============ -->\n      <section id=\"contributions\" aria-labelledby=\"h-contributions\">\n        <span class=\"sec-mark\">01</span>\n        <h2 id=\"h-contributions\">Contributions</h2>\n        <p class=\"sec-lede\">Five results, stated as the evidence supports them.</p>\n\n        <div class=\"cards\">\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">01</span>\n            <h3>The Screen</h3>\n            <p>14 of 16 registered candidate metrics executed on 23 graded checkpoints from 8 architecture families. Under six selection rules, one candidate passes all six: twin d-prime (C12, rho = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]). Self-ablation sensitivity (C2, rho = 0.90) clears amended rules, but its three surviving variants (C2, C2n, C17) are monotone transforms of one measurement.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">02</span>\n            <h3>Two-Sided Ground Truth</h3>\n            <p>23 checkpoints scored on the 94-item CORE-94 set (66 harmful, 28 XSTest-safe) with 64-token greedy decoding and a Gemini-2.5-Flash stance judge. A secondary judge (GPT-5-mini) agrees at kappa = 0.72. A blanket refuser scores S<sub>2</sub> = 0.5, not 1.0.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">03</span>\n            <h3>AMS Incumbent Comparison</h3>\n            <p>Every variant of the published AMS metric correlates worse than C2 with two-sided safety, with paired confidence intervals excluding zero. The reference implementation (ams-scanner 0.1.3) contains a right-padding bug that reads PAD-token activations.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">04</span>\n            <h3>Content-Free Pull Control</h3>\n            <p>After subtracting a norm-matched random steer from C1, the corrected metric (C1n) correlates at rho = 0.76, essentially unchanged (rho(C1, C1n) = 0.995), refuting the hypothesis that C1's signal is a content-free pull toward refusal.</p>\n          </article>\n\n          <article class=\"card\">\n            <span class=\"num\">05</span>\n            <h3>Grader-Side Refusal</h3>\n            <p>LLM judges under the StrongREJECT rubric assign the degenerate score tuple (1,1,1) to 65.9% of harmful items, with 328 vs. 67 discordant items against a stance-based framing (McNemar p &lt; 10<sup>-42</sup>).</p>\n          </article>\n        </div>\n      </section>\n\n      <!-- ============ METHOD ============ -->\n      <section id=\"method\" aria-labelledby=\"h-method\">", "numLines": 200, "startLine": 400, "totalLines": 901}}

{"type": "text", "file": {"filePath": "/ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_fcYd_7ruOwtm/4_gen_paper_repo/_4_assemble_paper/paper/index.html", "content": "        <span class=\"sec-mark\">02</span>\n        <h2 id=\"h-method\">Method</h2>\n        <p class=\"sec-lede\">One checkpoint in, one number out, with the ground truth and the rules fixed before any candidate was scored.</p>\n\n        <figure>\n          <button type=\"button\" class=\"figframe\" data-fig=\"0\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: pipeline overview\">\n            <img src=\"figures/fig_overview_v0.jpg\" alt=\"Pipeline diagram: 16 pre-registered candidate metrics, 14 of them executed, read weights or activations from each of 23 graded checkpoints on the 16-prompt SCREEN16 set; in parallel the CORE-94 set of 94 prompts is generated at 64 tokens and scored by a stance judge into the balanced safety target; six selection rules then filter the candidates down to one survivor, C12.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n          </button>\n          <figcaption><b>Pipeline overview.</b> Candidates read a single checkpoint on at most 16 prompts; the target is scored separately by generation and judging; six frozen rules decide what survives.</figcaption>\n        </figure>\n\n        <h3>Two-sided ground truth</h3>\n        <p>The target is balanced safety: S<sub>2</sub> = 0.5 &times; (harm-refusal rate) + 0.5 &times; (benign-compliance rate), computed on CORE-94, a set of 66 harmful items and 28 XSTest-safe items. Both failure modes cost the same. A model that refuses everything scores 0.5, and so does a model that complies with everything. That is the point of the two-sidedness: a one-sided refusal rate would reward a blanket refuser with a perfect score.</p>\n\n        <h3>Panel</h3>\n        <p>36 checkpoints from 8 architecture families (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, TinyLlama, Llama-3.2, OLMo-2, SmolLM2, Falcon3, Danube3), of which 23 are graded. All are at most 4B parameters and run in bf16, which is what makes a panel of this width affordable at all.</p>\n\n        <h3>Candidates</h3>\n        <p>16 candidate metrics in 7 families. Each one reads hidden states or weights on at most 16 prompts, the SCREEN16 set, and none of them generates text. Two behavioural quantities enter as bars rather than as candidates: the logit gap and refusal mass. A candidate has to beat them, not merely correlate.</p>\n\n        <h3>Six selection rules</h3>\n        <ol class=\"plain\">\n          <li><b>S1, incremental signal.</b> The candidate adds information beyond the cheap behavioural bars.</li>\n          <li><b>S2, direction specificity.</b> The signal is tied to the harm direction, not to any direction.</li>\n          <li><b>S3, pole control.</b> The metric responds to the safety pole rather than to generic prompt structure.</li>\n          <li><b>S4, sign agreement.</b> The correlation points the same way across subsets.</li>\n          <li><b>S5, efficiency.</b> The read is cheap enough to be worth doing.</li>\n          <li><b>S6, beyond confounds.</b> The relation survives known nuisance variables.</li>\n        </ol>\n        <p>The rules were frozen before scoring. That is what lets a single survivor mean something: C12 was not chosen after looking at which candidate won.</p>\n      </section>\n\n      <!-- ============ RESULTS ============ -->\n      <section id=\"results\" aria-labelledby=\"h-results\">\n        <span class=\"sec-mark\">03</span>\n        <h2 id=\"h-results\">Results</h2>\n        <p class=\"sec-lede\">One metric passes every rule. A different metric correlates far better and fails on specificity. Neither beats the behavioural ceiling.</p>\n\n        <div class=\"statgrid\">\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">0.61</span><span class=\"lbl\">C12 rho against balanced safety [0.36, 0.87]</span></div>\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">0.90</span><span class=\"lbl\">C2 rho, strongest raw correlation [0.79, 0.97]</span></div>\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">0.93</span><span class=\"lbl\">rho of 16 judged completions with full CORE-94</span></div>\n          <div class=\"stat\"><span class=\"val\">1 of 14</span><span class=\"lbl\">executed candidates passing all six rules</span></div>\n        </div>\n\n        <h3>The sole survivor</h3>\n        <p>C12, twin d-prime, reaches rho = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87] against balanced safety, with partial rho = 0.43 and a one-sided bound of 0.006. It is the only candidate to clear all six pre-registered rules.</p>\n        <p>The within-family picture is mixed in a way worth stating plainly. C12 is significant within Qwen3 (rho = 0.67, n = 8) and within Qwen2.5 (rho = 0.70, n = 5). It is not within TinyLlama (rho = -0.10, n = 5). A metric that works inside two families and reverses sign inside a third is not yet a general instrument.</p>\n\n        <figure>\n          <button type=\"button\" class=\"figframe\" data-fig=\"1\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: C12 twin d-prime versus balanced safety\">\n            <img src=\"figures/fig_c12_scatter_v0.png\" alt=\"Scatter plot of C12 twin d-prime on the horizontal axis against balanced safety S2 on the vertical axis for 23 graded checkpoints, with points coloured by architecture family; the cloud rises to the right with substantial spread, and values are spread across the range rather than clustered at zero.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n          </button>\n          <figcaption><b>C12 twin d-prime vs balanced safety.</b> Scatter plot of C12 (twin d-prime) versus balanced safety (S<sub>2</sub>) for the 23 graded checkpoints, coloured by architecture family. C12 is the sole candidate to pass all six selection rules, with Spearman rho = 0.61 [0.36, 0.87]. Unlike C2, C12's values are more evenly distributed: 12 of 23 models exceed the random-direction null.</figcaption>\n        </figure>\n\n        <h3>The strongest correlation</h3>\n        <p>C2, self-ablation sensitivity, reaches rho = 0.90 [0.79, 0.97], and exceeds the logit gap by 0.128 [0.012, 0.410]. As a detector of models with an ablatable harm direction it reaches AUROC = 0.96. But its distribution is close to binary, and within the 10 models that exceed the null the restricted correlation falls to rho = 0.64. C2 is largely telling you whether a harm direction exists to ablate, and only secondarily how safe the model is.</p>\n\n        <figure>\n          <button type=\"button\" class=\"figframe\" data-fig=\"2\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: C2 self-ablation versus balanced safety\">\n            <img src=\"figures/fig_screen_scatter_v0.png\" alt=\"Scatter plot of C2 self-ablation sensitivity on the horizontal axis against balanced safety S2 on the vertical axis for 23 graded checkpoints, coloured by architecture family; a dense cluster of points sits near zero on the left and a separate group lies to the right of a dashed vertical line marking absolute C2 equal to 0.1.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n          </button>\n          <figcaption><b>C2 self-ablation vs balanced safety.</b> Scatter plot of C2 (self-ablation sensitivity) versus balanced safety (S<sub>2</sub>) for the 23 graded checkpoints. Points are coloured by architecture family. C2 achieves Spearman rho = 0.90 [0.79, 0.97]. The plot reveals a near-binary split: 10 of 23 models have |C2| &gt; 0.1 (right cluster), while 13 cluster near zero.
